newsitem.title: CHINA: China says Hong Kong constitution guards freedoms.
newsitem.headline: China says Hong Kong constitution guards freedoms.

text.p: China on Thursday praised the future constitution it drafted for Hong Kong and said the document would ensure freedom of speech and press.
It also said there should be no hasty revisions of the constitution, known as the Basic Law, after the transfer of power on July 1.
The remarks, reported by the official Xinhua news agency, were made at a seminar marking the seventh anniversary of China's drafting of the future constitution for Hong Kong.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule on July 1 after more than 150 years as a British colony.
Under a Sino-British accord, Beijing has pledged to give the territory a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the handover.
The seminar followed criticism by activists in Hong Kong and by the United States and Britain of Beijing's plans to curtail some of the territory's civil liberties.
Beijing has said it will dismantle the territory's elected legislature and replace it with an appointed provisional body once it regains sovereignty.
Journalists in Hong Kong have expressed alarm over self-censorship by the media even before China regains control.
Xinhua quoted Zeng Jianhui, information office director at the State Council, or cabinet, as saying that the Basic Law fully protected freedom of the press.

He added that methods used to manage the media in China would not be used in Hong Kong, and the territory "will act in accordance with its original system and rules of operation". He did not elaborate.
China uses the Communist Party propaganda machine to enforce discipline on the domestic media, dictating what stories should be reported and how much prominence they should be given.
In the past, it has jailed journalists, accusing them of leaking state secrets, for giving unpublished information to foreign reporters.
Much of what Beijing considers to be secret would be viewed as routine public information in the West.
Another official at the seminar said mainland Chinese would not be able to travel to Hong Kong and set up representative offices without restriction after the transfer of power.
He did not elaborate but there has been concern in Hong Kong over regional Chinese governments sending officials to the territory and interfering in policy making.
